original.title: Ἀγαθὰ καὶ κακά.
paragraphs: Ὑπὸ τῶν κακῶν τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐδιώχθη ὡς ἀσθενῆ ὅντα:
εἰς οὐρανὸν δὲ ἀνῆλθεν.
Τὰ δὲ ἀγαθὰ ἠρώτησαν τὸν Δία πῶς εἶναι μετ'ἀνθρώπων.
Ὁ δὲ εἶπεν <μὴ> μετ' ἀλλήλων πάντα,
ἓν δὲ καθ' ἓν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἐπέρχεσθαι.
Διὰ τοῦτο τὰ μὲν κακὰ συνεχῆ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις,
ὡς πλησίον ὄντα, ἐπέρχεται,
τὰ δὲ ἀγαθὰ βράδιον,
ἐξ οὐρανοῦ κατιόντα.
Ὅτι ἀγαθῶν μὲν οὐδεὶς ταχέως ἐπιτυγχάνει,
ὑπὸ δὲ τῶν κακῶν ἕκαστος καθ' ἑκάστην πλήττεται.

translation.title: Blessings and Misfortunes
paragraphs: Blessings were driven away by Misfortunes on the grounds that they were weak;
they ascended to heaven.
The Blessings asked Zeus how they might exist among humans.
He replied that they should not all go together,
but rather that each should come to humans one by one.
For this reason, Misfortunes befall humans continuously,
being close by,
whereas blessings arrive more slowly,
descending from heaven.
This illustrates that no one attains blessings quickly,
while everyone is struck by misfortunes at every turn.

transliteration.title: The_Blessings and the_Misfortunes
paragraphs: The_Misfortunes once expelled the_Blessings because ‹they_were› weak;
‹they_raised› to heaven.
The_blessings asked Manwë how ‹they_will_exist› may among Men.
He replied ‹to_them› that not together ‹they_will_go› should,
but rather that each ‹will_come› to_Men one each time.
For reason this, misfortunes happen ever against men,
being ‹close_by›
while blessings come ‹more_slow›,
descending from heaven.
This illuminates that ‹no_one› obtains fast blessings,
while everyone suffer by misfortunes ‹many_times›.

roman.title: In·elvair ah in·egmoer
paragraphs: In·egmoer erlu ennistanner in·elvair añ_gaeth_i nîr wisg;
erianner na venel.
In·elvair vabenner Manwe movan dhathar ce mig Edain.
Te dambent andin i ú vinegel menathar aen,
ach hennui i ail tolatha n'Edain min ail lû.
Añ gaeth hen, egmoer chídar ui dan Edain,
nîl edos,
lo elvair delir eñgwir,
duiad o venel.
Se gelia i alphen gêd lim elvair,
lo ilphen negelir vo egmoer lael.
